title: A mixing time method for estimating the sample complexity of quantum state discrimination
abstract: We develop a mixing time method for estimating the sample complexity of quantum state discrimination. We start with considering the minimum-error discrimination of geometrically uniform pure state ensembles, and prove that its sample complexity has a tight estimate given by a quantum homogeneous mixing time [George et al., 2026] and a quantum version of the generalized Dobrushin coefficient [Wolfer, 2020]. This quantum mixing time further reduces to a classical one when the generating group $G$ forms a Gelfand pair with the stabilizer subgroup $H$ of the generator state. In this case the generalized Dobrushin coefficient can be fully expressed by representation-theoretic quantities of the commutative Hecke algebra $\operatorname{End}_G(\mathbb C[G/H])$. In particular, this method reduces the sample complexity estimation of learning quantum coupon collector states [Arunachalam et al., 2020] and learning phase states to classical mixing time problems. We apply this framework to answer the open problems of learning degree-$d$ phase states over $\mathbb F_q$ in [Alrabiah et al., 2026] and generalized Boolean phase states over $\mathbb Z_q$ [Arunachalam et al., 2023]. The framework also applies to hypergraph state ensembles, giving estimates expressed fully in terms of hypergraph data and recovering estimates for graph state ensembles in [Montanaro and Shao, 2022]. Finally, we extend the discussion to arbitrary mixed state ensembles with uniform priors, prove a sandwiched bound for minimum-error discrimination sample complexity by a quantum weakly mixing time, and provide a tight estimate for the minimax discrimination sample complexity from [D'Ariano et al., 2005] by a Dobrushin-type coefficient. We also discuss the method of strengthened data processing inequality [Gao and Rouz{é}, 2022] and give an upper bound in terms of a strengthened data processing inequality constant.
summary: This work introduces a mixing time method to estimate the sample complexity for quantum state discrimination. By relating the problem to the mixing time of a quantum random walk, the authors derive tight bounds using generalized Dobrushin coefficients. This framework successfully estimates complexity for diverse quantum ensembles, including phase and hypergraph states.
main_problem: The paper develops a method to estimate the sample complexity required for minimum-error quantum state discrimination.
main_result: The sample complexity is shown to be tightly bounded by quantum mixing times and generalized Dobrushin coefficients, providing explicit estimates for various state ensembles.
method: The core method involves relating the state discrimination problem to the mixing time of a quantum Markov random walk, utilizing concepts from harmonic analysis and representation theory.
model_or_system: The analysis covers geometrically uniform pure state ensembles, general mixed state ensembles, and specific structured ensembles like phase states and hypergraph states.
key_observables: Sample complexity ($k_{\min}$), quantum mixing time ($t_{\min}$), and the generalized Dobrushin coefficient ($\kappa_{	ext{gen}}$).
important_parameters: Error parameter ($\epsilon$), the structure of the generating group $G$, and the stabilizer subgroup $H$.
main_assumptions: The initial analysis focuses on uniform prior ensembles, but the framework is extended to arbitrary mixed states. A reduction to classical mixing time requires the generating group to form a Gelfand pair.
figures_summary: A summary table (TABLE I) compiles results linking various ensemble types (e.g., Gelfand-pair, Feature-map phase states) to their respective mixing formulations and complexity bounds.
paper_structure: The paper builds from the general problem of state discrimination to specific cases (GU pure states, Gelfand pairs), deriving bounds using mixing times, and finally extending the analysis to arbitrary mixed states using strengthened data processing inequalities.
why_interesting: It provides powerful, mathematically rigorous tools (mixing times, Dobrushin coefficients) to estimate fundamental resource requirements (sample complexity) in quantum information tasks, bridging quantum dynamics with classical information theory bounds.
